name: price-their-work
style: Confident, punchy narrator for a short-form finance video. Energetic but clear, natural conversational pace. Direct and slightly provocative. Crisp emphasis on numbers. Take a short beat between lines.

lines.text: How poor versus rich people price their work.
A poor person cleans houses for twenty-five dollars an hour.
Not because the market decided that.
Because they did.
Ten houses a week, three hours each.
Thirty hours of cleaning.
Plus ten hours of driving between houses, unpaid.
Plus sixty dollars of supplies, from their own pocket.
Do the math they refuse to do.
Seven hundred fifty dollars in.
Minus sixty for supplies.
Six hundred ninety left.
For forty hours of work.
Seventeen dollars and twenty-five cents an hour.
They call it hard work.
It's not hard work.
It's cheap work with long hours.
When a client asks for a discount, they say yes,
then complain about cheap clients behind their back.
Nobody forced that discount.
They volunteered it.
When the far house calls, forty-five minutes away, they say yes too.
They don't have a pricing problem.
They have a backbone problem.
Here's what a rich person does with the same mop and bucket.
First, they raise the price to forty dollars an hour, new inquiries only.
Two cheap clients leave.
Good.
Those two were never customers.
They were charity cases.
Second, they kill hourly pricing completely.
One hundred forty dollars per house, flat.
Two and a half hours with their system.
Fifty-six dollars an hour.
Clients don't buy hours.
They buy a clean house.
Price the house.
Third, they fire the two farthest houses and take two on the same street.
Driving drops to zero.
The distance was never the client's problem.
It was theirs.
Fourth, one upsell.
Fridge clean. Thirty dollars. Fifteen minutes.
Four out of eight say yes.
One hundred twenty dollars extra. Every week.
Now the real math.
Eight houses times one hundred forty: one thousand one hundred twenty.
Plus one hundred twenty in upsells.
One thousand two hundred forty dollars.
Twenty hours. Zero driving.
Sixty-two dollars an hour.
Nobody underpays you.
You underprice you.
Poor people sell hours and blame the market.
Rich people sell outcomes and set the market.
Same mop, opposite price tag.
